newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish parliament sees cross-border bank mergers.
newsitem.headline: Finnish parliament sees cross-border bank mergers.

text.p: Cross-border mergers between banks seeking greater efficiency are likely to result from European monetary union, the Finnish parliament's economic committee said in a statement received on Friday.
"The physical location of banks will be of less and less importance in the future," the committee said referring to the EMU environment scheduled to begin in January 1999.
Initially, mergers would take place inside EMU countries.
"Gradually, as market shares are being increased and benefits of economies of scale sought, bank mergers across borders are likely to become more common," the committee said.
Its statement is the legislature's response to a government report to parliament on state support to banks and will form the base for a plenary debate on Saturday.
EMU would bring tougher competition in many areas of the banking business and eliminate some means of generating revenue, for example through lower foreign exchange trading volumes.

Mergers between banks and insurance companies into financial service warehouses were also possible, the committee said, adding the EU Commission was working on rules for the supervision of and minimum requirements for financial conglomerates.
Finnish banks were "quite inefficient" compared to other Nordic banks, the committee said.
Facing tougher competition in the future, Finnish banks should not count on higher net interest margins nor on any further significant fall in credit losses, it said.
"A permanent improvement of the profitability of domestic banks is to a large extent up to how well they succeed in trimming their costs," it added.
While cutting costs, banks should at the same time improve and diversify the range of services on offer -- and control the risks related to new products, the committee said.

"The effects of increasing competition brought by EMU will first be visible on the capital markets. As a result of EMU, the capital market funding needs of domestic banks will become even more dependent on big international banks," the committee said.
